subject: ss-plastic-surgery
title: Nasoorbitoethmoid Complex and Orbital Blowout Fractures

steps.say: Nasoorbitoethmoid fractures are smashing the midface core where the nasal bones, eye sockets, and ethmoid air cells converge. The pivotal structure is the central bone shard carrying the medial canthal tendon, and the whole fixation plan is hinging on whether that shard stays in one piece. Surgeons are typing every NOE pattern by the fate of this tendon-bearing piece.
steps.tx: **Nasoorbitoethmoid (NOE) fractures** shatter the central midface where the nose, orbits, and ethmoid meet. The critical structure is the central **tendon-bearing bone fragment** carrying the **medial canthal tendon (MCT)**. Whether that fragment and its **tendon insertion** survive intact is deciding the entire **repair strategy**.

rows: Decides the Markowitz and Manson type

steps.say: Markowitz and Manson are grading NOE fractures by the fate of the central fragment. Type one is a single large fragment with the tendon still attached, type two is comminuted but keeping the insertion intact, and type three is severe comminution with frank tendon avulsion. Higher types are demanding more complex canthal fixation.
steps.tx: **Markowitz and Manson** classify NOE fractures into **Type I** with a single large **central fragment**, **Type II** with a **comminuted** fragment but intact **MCT insertion**, and **Type III** with severe comminution plus **MCT avulsion**. The type is dictating whether simple **fixation** or formal **canthal reattachment** follows.

The image shows an axial scan plus 3D inset labeled **Markowitz Manson Type II** with scattered **comminution** yet a marked **MCT insertion** on the central fragment. Intact insertion means fixation can use the fragment rather than full tendon reattachment. Read comminution with insertion status together because the pair sets the repair plan.
steps.say: This scan looks down through the midface with labels pointing to broken bits around the nose and the central piece near the eye. The inset skull view marks the same central fragment and the tendon anchor point. Even though the bone is shattered into pieces, the anchor is still attached. That attached anchor allows simpler fixation, which is why Type Two sits between simple and complex.

vis.alt: Axial CT plus skull inset showing midface comminution with the central fragment and tendon insertion marked as Type Two.
vis.caption: Comminuted midface with intact tendon anchor, Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Traumatic telecanthus is widening the intercanthal distance beyond thirty five millimetres as the canthal-bearing fragments splay apart. The nasal dorsum is sinking into a saddle nose shape, while a cribriform dural tear is leaking fluid as CSF rhinorrhoea. These three hallmarks are declaring an NOE fracture at the bedside.
steps.tx: Clinical hallmarks of NOE fractures include traumatic **telecanthus** with **intercanthal distance** over **35 mm**, **saddle nose** deformity from dorsal collapse, and **CSF rhinorrhoea** from **cribriform** dural tears. Splaying of the **canthal-bearing fragments** widens the distance, while the **nasal dorsum** sinks into a saddle.

steps.say: A blunt impact on the globe is raising intraorbital pressure until the thinnest wall gives way. The break is involving the thin posteromedial orbital floor just behind the rim, often extending into the lamina papyracea medially. The bank figure is displaying the blowout with entrapped muscle beside the Le Fort fracture lines.
steps.tx: **Orbital blowout** fracture follows blunt globe impact raising **intraorbital pressure** until the thinnest wall fails. The break most commonly involves the thin **posteromedial orbital floor**, often extending into the **lamina papyracea** of the **ethmoid bone**. The **infraorbital rim** usually stays intact while the floor gives way.

vis.alt: Anterior skull showing transverse maxillary, pyramidal, and craniofacial disjunction fracture lines with an orbital floor blowout and entrapped muscle.
vis.caption: Facial fracture patterns with blowout and muscle entrapment. Thresholds and timing are in the text, not on the drawing (StewardMD).

steps.say: The inferior rectus or inferior oblique muscle is catching in the floor defect and causing vertical double vision that worsens when looking upward. The forced duction test is turning positive because the globe cannot move freely. Periorbital bruising with infraorbital numbness is completing the entrapment picture.
steps.tx: Entrapment of the **inferior rectus** or **inferior oblique** muscle causes vertical **diplopia** on upward gaze with a positive **forced duction test**. The tethered globe cannot follow the finger, while **periorbital ecchymosis** and **infraorbital paraesthesia** mark the **floor defect** clinically and confirm the **entrapment**.

steps.say: The white-eyed blowout in children is presenting a deceptively quiet eye while hiding an entrapped muscle. The trapped tissue is triggering the oculocardiac reflex through vagal stimulation, causing bradycardia with nausea and syncope. This life-threatening reflex is making the injury a surgical emergency needing release within hours.
steps.tx: **White-eyed blowout** fracture in children is a **surgical emergency** hiding an entrapped muscle behind a quiet eye. The trapped tissue triggers the **oculocardiac reflex**, causing life-threatening **bradycardia** with nausea, vomiting, and **syncope**. **Vagal stimulation** drives the reflex, so release cannot wait.

steps.say: Surgeons are repairing blowouts within two weeks when diplopia persists with a positive forced duction test. Enophthalmos exceeding two millimetres from enlarged orbital volume is mandating surgery, as is a floor defect exceeding fifty percent of the orbital floor. Smaller defects without entrapment are settling with observation.
steps.tx: **Orbital floor repair** within **2 weeks** follows persistent **diplopia** with positive **forced duction**, **enophthalmos** exceeding **2 mm**, or a **floor defect** exceeding **50%** of the **orbital floor**. Enlarged **orbital volume** sinks the globe, while smaller defects without entrapment settle with **observation**.

steps.say: Reconstruction is rebuilding the floor with autologous bone or cartilage grafts for smaller defects. Larger defects are receiving porous polyethylene Medpor sheets or titanium mesh for lasting support. The transconjunctival route is hiding the scar inside the eyelid, while the subciliary route is running just below the lashes for wider exposure.
steps.tx: Floor defects are rebuilt with the patient's own **bone or cartilage** when small, while **porous polyethylene (Medpor)** sheets and **titanium** mesh support larger defects. Surgeons reach the floor through a **transconjunctival** incision hidden inside the eyelid, or through a **subciliary** incision below the lashes for wider exposure. **Transnasal wiring** restores the distance in NOE patterns.
